problem: Breast cancer histopathology classification (benign vs malignant) from microscopic tissue images is a labor-intensive task for pathologists. Automated image analysis can provide a supporting second opinion, but different representation-learning approaches (task-specific CNNs vs general-purpose foundation models) have different strengths.
gap_motivation: CNNs like EfficientNet learn domain-specific visual features through supervised fine-tuning, while foundation models like DINOv2 learn general-purpose visual representations through large-scale self-supervised pretraining, without ever seeing this dataset. It is not obvious in advance whether these two representations are redundant or complementary -- this project tests that empirically.
method: EfficientNet-B0 was fine-tuned end-to-end as the CNN baseline. DINOv2 ViT-S/14 was kept frozen and used purely as a feature extractor (no fine-tuning), producing 384-D embeddings for every image.
fusion: The 1280-D CNN backbone feature and 384-D DINOv2 embedding were each projected via a Linear-ReLU-Dropout layer to a shared 256-D space, then concatenated into a 512-D fused vector, followed by a shallow classifier (both source models kept frozen during fusion training).
grouping: BreakHis provides multiple images per patient (82 unique patients, not true WSI slides). Patient/group-aware attention aggregation combined per-image fused representations within a patient using a gated-attention mechanism, producing one prediction per patient rather than per image.
ensemble: A weighted average of CNN, Foundation-only, and Fusion probabilities was tested. Weights were grid-searched using ONLY the validation set (test set was never touched during weight selection), to avoid any test-set leakage into model selection.
explainability: Grad-CAM was applied to the CNN backbone (shared by the CNN baseline and Fusion's CNN branch) on 8 representative test images spanning correct and incorrect predictions for both classes. Attention weights from the grouped model were also visualized for one test patient, showing a concentrated (non-uniform) weighting pattern across that patient's images.
robustness: The CNN was evaluated under two controlled input perturbations. It was fairly robust to mild Gaussian noise (AUROC 0.9062 → 0.9032) but more sensitive to Gaussian blur (AUROC 0.9062 → 0.8713), with predictions shifting toward malignant under blur (higher sensitivity, lower specificity).
result: CNN + Foundation Fusion produced the strongest, most balanced performance among the directly-comparable (full test set, n=1395) experiments: AUROC 0.9087, F1 0.9255, Accuracy 0.8968, Sensitivity 0.9227. The validation-weighted ensemble did not improve over the best individual model (it collapsed entirely to Foundation-only). Attention/grouped aggregation showed promising sensitivity (1.0) and F1 (0.9474) but at only 13 test groups, providing exploratory rather than conclusive evidence.
limitations: This is a patch/image-level pipeline using patient/group identifiers, NOT a true Whole-Slide Image (WSI) pipeline -- there is no slide-level spatial structure or coordinates. AUROC improvements from fusion are modest (not dramatic). Grad-CAM explains only the CNN pathway, not the DINOv2 branch. Attention/grouped results rest on a very small test group count. No clinical validation, diagnostic-readiness, or deployment claims are made -- this is a research prototype.
